title: Both Parents' Vitamin B12 Levels Linked to Birth Defect Risk, Major Study Finds
excerpt: A large prospective study from China shows that higher B12 in fathers — not just mothers — before conception is associated with fewer birth defects, a finding with outsized implications for India's B12-deficient population.
body:
• A prospective cohort study of over 3,000 couples and 17,765 women found that higher vitamin B12 levels in both parents before conception were associated with a lower risk of birth defects.
  • The study, published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, is among the first to quantify the role of paternal B12 status in preventing birth defects — shifting the focus beyond maternal nutrition alone.
  • The findings carry particular weight for India, where vitamin B12 deficiency affects an estimated 40–75% of the population, driven largely by vegetarian and near-vegetarian diets.
  • India has one of the world's highest rates of neural tube defects, with an estimated 115,000 preventable cases annually, according to prior population-based studies.

A Study That Changes the Equation

A large prospective study from China has found that higher vitamin B12 levels in both parents around the time of conception are associated with a significantly lower risk of birth defects — a finding that extends the conversation about preconception nutrition well beyond mothers.

Researchers from the Children's Hospital of Fudan University and colleagues used the Shanghai Preconception Cohort to study 3,032 couples who provided blood samples within four months before conception and 17,765 women tested at four months' gestation or earlier. The study measured vitamin B12 and red blood cell (RBC) folate levels and examined their relationship with birth defects identified among live births, stillbirths and pregnancies ending because of fetal abnormalities.

The results, published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, showed that higher preconception maternal and paternal vitamin B12 levels were both associated with a lower predicted prevalence of birth defects. Mothers with adequate RBC folate levels in early pregnancy also showed lower risk.

"These findings support the potential importance of both paternal and maternal nutrition during the periconceptional period and early pregnancy."

— Annals of Internal Medicine, study authors

Why Paternal Nutrition Matters

Public health messaging around pregnancy has long centred on maternal nutrition — prenatal vitamins, folate supplements and dietary guidelines are almost universally directed at mothers. The role of the father's nutritional status has received far less attention.

This study adds to a growing body of evidence suggesting that paternal nutrition at the time of conception plays a more significant role than previously understood. Vitamin B12 is essential for DNA synthesis and methylation, processes critical to sperm quality and early embryonic development. Earlier, smaller studies had hinted at this link — a study from India found that fathers of children with neural tube defects had significantly lower folate and vitamin B12 levels and higher homocysteine compared to fathers of unaffected children.

The Shanghai study's scale and prospective design give it considerably more weight than earlier case-control analyses.

India's B12 Crisis Makes This Personal

The findings carry outsized implications for the Indian diaspora and for India itself, where vitamin B12 deficiency is endemic. An estimated three-quarters of the Indian population — vegetarians and non-vegetarians alike — are deficient in B12, according to studies published in BMJ Nutrition, Prevention & Health. Among pregnant women in India, deficiency prevalence ranges from 40% to 70%.

The consequences are severe. India has one of the world's highest rates of neural tube defects (NTDs). A population-based study in Uttar Pradesh found 8.2 affected babies per 1,000 live births — among the highest globally. A follow-up study in the same state years later confirmed the rate remained persistently high at 7.48 per 1,000. With approximately 26 million births annually in India, researchers have estimated that a robust preconception nutrition programme could prevent approximately 115,000 NTD births every year.

The vegetarian and near-vegetarian diets common across much of India are a primary driver. Vitamin B12 is found naturally only in animal products — meat, fish, eggs and dairy. While dairy consumption provides some B12, the levels are often insufficient to prevent deficiency, particularly among those with limited access to diverse animal-source foods.

Beyond Folate: A Two-Vitamin Problem

For decades, folate supplementation has been the cornerstone of NTD prevention worldwide. Many countries mandate folic acid fortification of flour. India, however, has no such mandate. More importantly, the new research suggests that folate alone may not be enough.

The intracellular enzyme methionine synthase — essential for the one-carbon metabolism pathway that prevents birth defects — requires both folate and vitamin B12 as cofactors. Without adequate B12, supplemental folate alone cannot be fully utilised by tissues, according to research from the BMJ Nutrition, Prevention & Health. This makes B12 not just an additional factor but a necessary one.

What This Means Going Forward

The study's authors call for greater attention to the nutritional status of both partners during the periconceptional period. For India, the message is clear: preconception care needs to include B12 screening and supplementation for both parents, not just folate for mothers.

Researchers have noted that Indian women of reproductive age show strong resistance to taking daily vitamin tablets but are open to consuming fortified staple foods. Tea fortified with folate and B12 has shown promise in preliminary studies as a culturally appropriate delivery mechanism. With 26 million births a year and some of the world's highest rates of preventable birth defects, the stakes for getting preconception nutrition right in India are enormous.
